questions.q: Why is a raw metric like "CPU is at 62%" meaningless on its own to a DBA?
options: Because you can't judge whether a number is abnormal without already knowing what normal looks like for that specific database — which is what a baseline provides
Because CPU percentage is never a useful metric for Azure SQL
Because Azure Monitor rounds all percentages to the nearest 10%
Because 62% is always considered a safe, healthy value regardless of context
questions.explain: A baseline turns a raw number into a comparison point: 95% CPU is only meaningful once you know this database normally runs at 60-70%.

questions.q: What three categories of data does a real performance baseline capture, per this lesson?
options: Typical CPU/DTU utilization by hour and day, query duration percentiles (not just averages), and the top wait statistics
Only the average CPU percentage over the last 24 hours
The number of tables, indexes, and stored procedures in the database
Only the total storage size of the database
questions.explain: Resource consumption, duration percentiles, and wait statistics together form the profile a DBA compares against during an incident.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize duration percentiles (p50/p95/p99) over the plain average query duration?
options: Because a handful of very slow outlier executions can hide inside an otherwise fine-looking average — p99 exposes the slow tail that the average masks
Because averages are mathematically impossible to calculate for query duration
Because percentiles are easier to calculate than averages in T-SQL
Because Azure SQL does not report average query duration at all
questions.explain: A query averaging 50ms with a p99 of 4 seconds is a very different problem than one steadily at 50ms — the average alone can't tell you that.

questions.q: Over what kind of time window should a baseline typically be captured, and why?
options: At least a full business cycle (e.g. a week including a known-heavy period), so it reflects normal variation instead of one quiet day
Exactly 60 seconds, since Azure Monitor only retains that much detail
A single random 5-minute window is always sufficient
Only during nighttime hours when the database is idle
questions.explain: A baseline captured on a lucky quiet Tuesday won't reflect real Monday-morning batch load or month-end spikes.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should a DBA re-establish a baseline?
options: After any major event that changes the workload — a new feature shipping, a traffic surge, or a table crossing a size threshold that changes query plans — and treat one older than a quarter with suspicion
Never — a baseline captured once is valid for the life of the database
Only when Microsoft releases a new version of SQL Server
Every single hour, regardless of whether anything changed
questions.explain: A baseline goes stale the moment the underlying workload changes, so it needs to be refreshed after events that plausibly shift normal behavior.
